category: Agent, instrument, means, manner, and measure

entries.meaning: Names the party whose request or order set the action going. It leaves the doer in place and adds a second, superior agent above them, which is why it is the standard phrase for reporting influence, pressure, and chains of command.
examples: The investigation was reopened at the behest of two members of the committee.
At the behest of the state, the district rewrote its attendance policy over the summer.
The clause was inserted at the behest of a single lender and nobody else read it closely.
She took the job at the behest of a mentor she could not say no to.
The audit was commissioned at his behest and delivered to him alone.
The park was renamed at the urging of a neighborhood association that had been asking for nine years.
entries.pronunciation note: at thuh bih-HEST uhv; weak /ət ðə bəˈhɛst əv/, and in running speech the of goes down to bare /ə/ — /ət ðə bəˈhɛst ə/
entries.русский: по настоянию, по требованию — называет того, чья воля вызвала действие
entries.register: formal to neutral; standard in journalism, history, and legal writing
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun, and like the other agent phrases the complement must be animate or institutional — a person, an office, an agency. Never a gerund, never a finite clause. It does not strand. With a pronoun, the possessive construction is commoner: at his behest rather than at the behest of him.
entries.pattern: [passive clause] at the behest of [instigator] · At the behest of [instigator], [clause] · [clause] at [possessive] behest
entries.variants: at the request of is the neutral everyday form, at the direction of makes it an order, and at the instance of is the courtroom formula; each has its own entry. At the urging of and at the insistence of grade the pressure upward without changing the construction, and at the instigation of is the most accusatory and the rarest.
entries.contrast: The one phrase in this section that names who ordered it rather than who did it. Plain by marks the hand; at the behest of marks the voice behind the hand, which is why the memo was written by a staffer at the behest of the governor can put two different agents in one sentence and no other construction can. Against on the part of: that phrase hangs an abstract noun on its doer, this one hangs a completed act on its instigator. Behest is a fossil noun exactly like dint in by dint of — it survives only inside this phrase, so it takes no plural and no modifier: ✗ a strong behest, ✗ at several behests.
entries.see also: by, at the direction of, at the request of, on the part of, at the hands of, by order of

entries.meaning: Names the person or body whose order produced the act, while leaving the doer in the sentence. It is the strongest of the phrases that separate the hand from the voice behind it, and it is reached for exactly when responsibility rather than authorship is the question.
examples: The files were destroyed at the direction of a supervisor who has since left the company.
At the direction of the court, the parties filed a joint status report on Friday.
The analysis was prepared at the direction of outside counsel and is being withheld as privileged.
Two of the payments were made at his direction, and about the third he says he knew nothing.
Troops were pulled back from the northern posts at the direction of the department, over the objection of the local commander.
The clinic began screening every patient at the direction of the state health office.
entries.pronunciation note: at thuh duh-REK-shun uhv; weak /ət ðə dəˈrɛkʃn əv/, casually /ət ðə dəˈrɛkʃn ə/ — the first vowel of direction is /ə/ for some American speakers and /aɪ/ for others, and both are standard
entries.русский: по указанию, по распоряжению — приказ, которого нельзя было ослушаться
entries.register: formal to neutral; legal, corporate, military, and journalistic — an American meets it in a deposition, an internal investigation report, and any news story about who told whom to do what
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun, and the complement must be animate or institutional — a person, an office, a court, counsel, a board. Never a gerund (✗ at the direction of closing the file), never a finite clause. It does not strand. With a pronoun the possessive is the normal shape: at his direction, at the court's direction.
entries.pattern: [passive clause] at the direction of [authority] · At the direction of [authority], [clause] · [clause] at [possessive] direction
entries.variants: by direction of is the military and official form and survives in signature blocks — By direction of the Commanding Officer, or simply By direction — and is written up with the official formulas at by order of. Do not swap it for under the direction of, which names continuous supervision (an orchestra under the direction of Marin Alsop) where this phrase names one order that produced one act.
entries.contrast: The mandatory member of the instigation family. At the request of leaves the doer free to decline, at the behest of applies pressure, and at the direction of removes the choice — which is why it is the one that carries legal weight. Whether a contractor acted at the direction of the company decides who answers for what he did, and whether a memo was prepared at the direction of counsel decides whether it is privileged. Against on behalf of: acting for somebody is not the same as acting on their orders. Against at the discretion of: an order already given, against a power that may never be exercised.
entries.see also: at the behest of, at the request of, at the discretion of, by order of, on behalf of

entries.meaning: Assigns the power of decision to a named party without obliging them to use it. Everything the phrase governs is optional by construction, and the reason for writing it into a document is to keep the decision from being second-guessed.
examples: Late fees may be waived at the discretion of the property manager.
Bonuses are awarded at the sole discretion of the compensation committee.
Sentencing within that range is at the discretion of the trial judge.
The course may be repeated once at the discretion of the department chair.
Shifts get assigned at the discretion of whoever is building the schedule that month.
The policy may be canceled at the company's discretion on thirty days' notice.
entries.pronunciation note: at thuh dih-SKRESH-un uhv; weak /ət ðə dəˈskrɛʃn əv/, casually /ət ðə dəˈskrɛʃn ə/ — four unstressed syllables around -skresh-
entries.русский: на усмотрение кого-л. — называет того, кто вправе решать, а не того, кто действовал
entries.register: formal; contracts, statutes, and policies — an American meets it in a lease, an employee handbook, a syllabus, and the fine print of a refund policy
entries.complement: noun phrase naming the party who gets to decide — a person, an officer, a board, a court, a company — or a fused relative standing in for one (at the discretion of whoever is on duty). Never a gerund, never a finite clause. With a pronoun or a name the possessive is normal: at his discretion, at the landlord's discretion. The intensified forms are fixed and come from drafting: at the sole discretion of, at the absolute discretion of, at its sole and absolute discretion.
entries.pattern: [may] [verb] at the discretion of [decider] · [noun phrase] at the sole discretion of [decider] · [clause] at [possessive] discretion
entries.contrast: Alone in this section it names nobody who acted. It names who holds the power to decide whether anything happens at all, which is why it attaches to may and will far more often than to a plain past tense: refunds may be issued at the discretion of the manager is the natural shape. In drafting it is the switch that turns a duty into an option, and sole and absolute get bolted on to keep a court from reading a reasonableness requirement into the power. Against subject to: subject to the approval of the board means somebody has to say yes; at the discretion of the board means somebody may say no and owes no reason. Against at the mercy of: the same imbalance of power, seen from underneath and with feeling.
entries.see also: at the direction of, subject to, at the mercy of, at, under the auspices of

entries.meaning: Attributes harm to a responsible party. The phrase is doing rhetorical work that plain by does not do: it foregrounds the agent, implies that the suffering was inflicted rather than merely caused, and invites the reader to assign blame. Sportswriting borrowed it for defeats, where the same framing turns a loss into something done to a team.
examples: Thousands died at the hands of the regime in the first eighteen months alone.
She described years of mistreatment at the hands of a supervisor everyone had complained about.
He lost the house at the hands of a servicer that had misplaced two years of payments.
The team suffered its worst loss in a decade at the hands of a program it had beaten nine straight times.
The bill died at the hands of a committee that never scheduled a hearing on it.
Her first campaign ended at the hands of an incumbent nobody thought was vulnerable.

senses.head: Suffering, injury, or death inflicted by someone
examples: Thousands died at the hands of the regime in the first eighteen months alone.
She described years of mistreatment at the hands of a supervisor everyone had complained about.
He lost the house at the hands of a servicer that had misplaced two years of payments.

senses.head: Defeat in a contest
examples: The team suffered its worst loss in a decade at the hands of a program it had beaten nine straight times.
The bill died at the hands of a committee that never scheduled a hearing on it.
Her first campaign ended at the hands of an incumbent nobody thought was vulnerable.

entries.pronunciation note: at thuh HANDZ uhv; weak /ət ðə ˈhændz əv/, and in running speech the of goes all the way down to bare /ə/ — /ət ðə ˈhændz ə/
entries.русский: от рук кого-л. — только о причинённом зле, гибели или поражении
entries.register: neutral to formal; heavy in journalism and history writing
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun, and the complement must be animate or institutional — a person, a group, a government, a team. Never a gerund, never a finite clause. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: [noun of suffering] at the hands of [agent] · [passive verb of suffering] at the hands of [agent]
entries.contrast: A specialized by. It marks the agent only of something bad — defeat, injury, humiliation, death — and it casts that agent as a perpetrator. He was killed by his brother is neutral reporting; He died at the hands of his brother is an accusation. Because the complement must be animate, it cannot cover instruments or natural forces: ✗ killed at the hands of a falling tree, ✗ flattened at the hands of the storm.
entries.see also: by, by the hand of, courtesy of, on the part of, through

entries.meaning: Names the party at whose urging or on whose application something was done. In American writing it now reads either as a quotation from an old record or as a deliberate archaism; in Scots law it remains the standard way to name the party who moved.
examples: The receiver was appointed at the instance of two of the bondholders.
The prosecution was brought at the instance of the collector of customs.
At the instance of the family, the coroner reopened the file.
The commission was created in 1887 at the instance of the grain shippers, who had been petitioning for a decade.
The action proceeds at the instance of the Lord Advocate, which is the Scottish formula word for word.
The clause was struck at the instance of a single creditor who had read it more carefully than anyone else.
entries.pronunciation note: at thee IN-stunss uhv; weak /ət ði ˈɪnstəns əv/, casually /ət ði ˈɪnstəns ə/
entries.русский: по ходатайству, по заявлению — устар., юр.; о стороне, по чьему обращению начато дело
entries.register: formal and legal, with an archaic flavor; an American meets it in nineteenth-century opinions, in histories that quote them, and in Scottish, Indian, and other Commonwealth legal writing, where it is still live. It is not current American prose — a modern American brief writes on the motion of or at the request of.
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun naming a party — a litigant, a prosecutor, a creditor, a government office. Never a gerund, never a finite clause. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: [proceeding] [brought / commenced] at the instance of [party] · [passive clause] at the instance of [party]
entries.variants: at the suit of is the older English formula for the same relation; on the motion of and at the request of are the modern American replacements.
entries.contrast: Watch the noun. Instance here is the old legal word for the urging or the application of a party — Latin instantia, "a pressing" — and not the ordinary modern noun meaning an example, which is why at the instance of the plaintiff means on the plaintiff's application and why a reader who knows only the modern noun hears the phrase as a mistake. It is the courtroom sibling of at the behest of and at the request of: the same relation between a party who asked and an act that followed, in a much narrower habitat. Do not confuse it with in the first instance or court of first instance, where instance means a stage of proceeding and no agent is named at all.
entries.see also: at the behest of, at the request of, at the direction of, ex parte, by order of

entries.meaning: Names the party who asked for what was then done. Asking is not ordering, so the doer's agency stays intact — which is why this is the safest of the agent-of-instigation phrases and, by a wide margin, the most common.
examples: The meeting was closed to the public at the request of two board members.
At the request of the university, the department released the raw scores.
The song was added to the program at the request of the family.
The records were sealed at her request and stayed sealed for thirty years.
The inspection was moved up at the request of the tenants' association.
He resigned from the committee at the request of the chairman, which everyone understood to mean something a good deal stronger.
entries.pronunciation note: at thuh rih-KWEST uhv; weak /ət ðə rəˈkwɛst əv/, casually /ət ðə rəˈkwɛst ə/
entries.русский: по просьбе — нейтральное указание на того, кто попросил
entries.register: neutral; the everyday member of the family, equally at home in journalism, business correspondence, and official prose
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun, animate or institutional, or a fused relative (at the request of whoever filed the complaint). Never a gerund — ✗ at the request of leaving early — and never a finite clause: ✗ at the request of she asked for it. It does not strand. With a pronoun the possessive is the normal form: at her request, at the family's request.
entries.pattern: [passive clause] at the request of [asker] · At the request of [asker], [clause] · [clause] at [possessive] request
entries.variants: by request and on request look like clipped versions of this phrase but are separate items with no complement at all — an encore by request, available on request — which makes them adverbials rather than prepositions. At your request is the correspondence form and at the request of counsel the standard legal one.
entries.contrast: The neutral center of the instigation family and the phrase to reach for when you are claiming nothing about pressure: at the behest of implies a superior pressing, at the urging of implies persuasion, at the direction of implies an order that could not be refused, and at the instance of moves the whole thing into a courtroom. Journalists use at the request of for exactly that neutrality — the name was withheld at the request of the family reports a fact and assigns no blame. Against courtesy of: the requester asked for an act, the supplier provided a thing.
entries.see also: at the behest of, at the direction of, at the instance of, courtesy of, on behalf of

entries.meaning: Credits an outcome to a benefactor's favor rather than to anybody's effort. In the formal use the benefactor is God and the claim is meant seriously; in modern American speech the same words are nearly always a wry admission that luck, or somebody else's kindness, did the work the speaker is being congratulated for.
examples: By the grace of God the herd came through the winter intact.
The cornerstone reads "Founded 1791, by the grace of Almighty God."
Charles III, by the Grace of God, King of the United Kingdom — a style whose wording has barely moved in five centuries.
By the grace of a sympathetic dispatcher, we got the last truck out of the yard.
He passed the class by the grace of a curve nobody has ever explained.
We had heat that week only by the grace of a neighbor with a generator and no sense of self-preservation.

senses.head: Through divine favor
examples: By the grace of God the herd came through the winter intact.
The cornerstone reads "Founded 1791, by the grace of Almighty God."
Charles III, by the Grace of God, King of the United Kingdom — a style whose wording has barely moved in five centuries.

senses.head: Thanks to somebody's undeserved help — light, often ironic
examples: By the grace of a sympathetic dispatcher, we got the last truck out of the yard.
He passed the class by the grace of a curve nobody has ever explained.
We had heat that week only by the grace of a neighbor with a generator and no sense of self-preservation.

entries.pronunciation note: by thuh GRAYSS uhv; weak /baɪ ðə ˈɡreɪs əv/, casually /baɪ ðə ˈɡreɪs ə/ — by keeps its full /aɪ/ and has no weak form of its own
entries.русский: милостью, по милости — божьей; в разг. речи иронично о везении или чужой помощи
entries.register: religious and formal in the literal sense; formulaic in royal and ecclesiastical styles; ironic or self-deprecating in ordinary modern American speech, which is where most Americans actually use it
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a benefactor — overwhelmingly God, and in the ironic use anybody credited with help the speaker does not think was earned (by the grace of a good mechanic, by the grace of whoever propped the door open). Never a gerund, never a finite clause. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: By the grace of God, [clause] · [name], by the Grace of God, [office] (the formula) · [clause] by the grace of [benefactor]
entries.variants: by the grace of God is the phrase for practical purposes. Latin Dei gratia, abbreviated D.G., is the same formula in royal styles and on coinage — which is where an American meets it, on Canadian coins reading D.G. Regina. The proverb there but for the grace of God go I is a separate idiom built on but for.
entries.contrast: It credits a benefactor's favor rather than anybody's labor, which is what separates it from plain by and from at the hands of. In the formulaic use it is a claim about where authority comes from: Charles III, by the Grace of God, King of the United Kingdom asserts that the crown was granted by no earthly body, and the phrase survives in that job on seals, coins, and episcopal signatures. In modern speech the same words nearly always do something lighter — crediting luck. Do not confuse it with with good grace (= gracefully, without complaint), which is a manner adverbial and a different phrase entirely.
entries.see also: by, courtesy of, thanks to, by virtue of, under the auspices of

entries.meaning: Attributes an act to the person who physically carried it out, usually as the instrument of somebody else. It survives in three narrow places: scripture and prose that echoes it, historical narrative about messengers and executioners, and the vocabulary of specialists arguing about which hand painted which sleeve.
examples: The law was given by the hand of Moses, in the formula the King James Bible uses a dozen times over.
The dispatch was sent by the hand of a courier who rode through the night.
The panel is now accepted as being by the hand of the master rather than the workshop.
He died by the hand of a man he had pardoned twice.
The marginal notes are by the hand of a later reader, probably a century after the text was copied.
The treaty reached the governor by the hand of his own son.
entries.pronunciation note: by thuh HAND uhv; weak /baɪ ðə ˈhænd əv/, casually /baɪ ðə ˈhænd ə/
entries.русский: рукой кого-л., через кого-л. — устар., книжн.; об исполнителе как орудии
entries.register: archaic and literary — the King James Bible and prose written in its shadow, and historical narrative; still live as a term of art in connoisseurship and manuscript cataloguing. Not ordinary modern usage, and a reader will hear any use of it as a deliberate borrowing.
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a person or a divine agent, or, in art and manuscript writing, an artist or a scribe. Never a gerund, never a finite clause. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: [passive clause] by the hand of [human instrument] · [message] [sent / delivered] by the hand of [messenger] · [work] by the hand of [artist]
entries.variants: at the hand of, singular, is the older biblical form for suffering received, and the living modern phrase is at the hands of — use that one. In the hand of is a different item and still current: it names the handwriting (a letter in the hand of Jefferson). Bare by hand, with no article and no complement, is a manner adverbial meaning not by machine and belongs to by.
entries.contrast: In the King James Bible the phrase marks the human instrument through whom a greater agent acted — the word of the Lord by the hand of Moses — and that flavor has never left it: the person named is a channel as much as an originator. Against at the hands of: the modern phrase attributes harm and assigns blame, this one attributes an act and does not, so he died at the hands of his brother accuses where he died by the hand of his brother narrates. Against plain by in art writing: a drawing by Rembrandt is an ordinary attribution, while by the hand of Rembrandt is a specific claim about who physically executed it, and it belongs with the graded cataloguing terms set out at after the manner of.
entries.see also: at the hands of, by, through, after the manner of, by and through

entries.respell: KUR-tuh-see uhv; weak /ˈkɚtəsi əv/, casually /ˈkɚtəsi ə/
entries.meaning: Credits the party that supplied, permitted, or provided the thing. Its native habitat is the small print under a photograph, but it has spread into ordinary prose in two directions: as a neutral attribution of a source, and — far more commonly in speech — as a sarcastic attribution of blame, where the "courtesy" is anything but.
examples: All images courtesy of the National Archives unless otherwise noted.
Data courtesy of the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Dinner was courtesy of the hotel, which had lost our reservation twice.
We spent the night in Denver, courtesy of a mechanical problem in Phoenix.
The winning run came courtesy of a throwing error by the shortstop.
He has a scar over his left eye courtesy of a hockey stick and a bad decision.

senses.head: Supplied or permitted by; with the permission of
examples: All images courtesy of the National Archives unless otherwise noted.
Data courtesy of the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Dinner was courtesy of the hotel, which had lost our reservation twice.

senses.head: Caused by — usually ironic, occasionally admiring
examples: We spent the night in Denver, courtesy of a mechanical problem in Phoenix.
The winning run came courtesy of a throwing error by the shortstop.
He has a scar over his left eye courtesy of a hockey stick and a bad decision.

entries.pronunciation note: which is one reason the bare credit-line form courtesy the Newberry Library got written down in the first place
entries.русский: с любезного разрешения, предоставлено кем-л.; иронично — «по милости» кого-л.
entries.register: neutral; standard in captions, credits, and journalism
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun naming a person, institution, or source. Never a gerund, never a finite clause. It frequently appears with no verb at all, as a freestanding credit line.
entries.pattern: [clause] courtesy of [source] · [noun phrase], courtesy of [source] · Courtesy of [source] (caption)
entries.variants: by courtesy of — older and more formal, still standard in British programs and exhibition labels. Bare courtesy with no of is normal American credit-line style: Photo courtesy Getty Images.
entries.contrast: Against by: by credits authorship, courtesy of credits permission or supply — a photograph by Ansel Adams versus a photograph courtesy of the Adams estate. Against thanks to: thanks to names a cause of an outcome; courtesy of names a giver. In the ironic use the two converge exactly, and both go sour on purpose: a two-hour delay courtesy of the FAA. This entry owns the credit-and-supply sense; the purely causal use (half of downtown was dry by noon, courtesy of a burst main) is written up with the prepositions of cause at courtesy of.
entries.see also: by, thanks to, at the hands of, through, courtesy of (cause)

entries.meaning: Assigns the doer of an abstract action to the noun that names it. Whenever a nominalization has swallowed a verb — negligence, reluctance, misstatement, effort — the subject of that buried verb has to be reattached somehow, and this is the formal way to do it.
examples: The report found no wrongdoing on the part of the responding officers.
There was real reluctance on the part of the faculty to move the deadline.
Any misstatement on the part of the applicant voids the policy.
It took months of quiet work on the part of two staffers to get the language drafted.
An error on the part of the pilot does not by itself establish negligence.
The delay reflected a genuine failure of nerve on the part of the leadership.
entries.pronunciation note: on thuh PART uhv; weak /ən ðə ˈpɑrt əv/, casually /ən ðə ˈpɑrt ə/
entries.русский: со стороны кого-л. — приписывает отглагольному существительному его деятеля
entries.register: formal; legal, academic, and bureaucratic prose
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun, always animate or institutional. Never a gerund, never a finite clause. With a pronoun, most writers switch to the possessive construction instead: on his part, for my part.
entries.pattern: [abstract noun of behavior] on the part of [agent] · On the part of [agent], [clause]
entries.contrast: It hangs an agent on an abstract noun — a failure, a decision, a reluctance — where by would be ambiguous: a failure by the board can be read as a failure the board caused, while a failure on the part of the board can only mean the board failed. That precision is why the phrase survives in legal writing, and nine times out of ten in ordinary prose the possessive is shorter and just as clear: the board's failure. Do not confuse it with on behalf of, which means representing, not committed by.
entries.see also: by, on behalf of, at the hands of, under the auspices of

entries.meaning: Puts an institution's name and protection behind an activity without saying that the institution performed it. The Roman augurs took the auspices before any public act, and the modern phrase keeps that structure exactly: somebody senior has looked the thing over and blessed it.
examples: The talks were held in Vienna under the auspices of the United Nations.
The dig has run every summer since 1974 under the auspices of the university's classics department.
The report was published under the auspices of a foundation that had funded none of the underlying research.
Vaccination clinics operated under the auspices of the county health department in four school gyms.
Under the auspices of the trade commission, the two sides met for the first time in a decade.
The exhibition traveled to six cities under the aegis of the Smithsonian.
entries.pronunciation note: UHN-der thee AW-spuh-siz uhv; weak /ˈʌndɚ ði ˈɔspəsəz əv/, casually /ˈʌndɚ ði ˈɔspəsəz ə/ — some American speakers have /ˈɑspəsɪz/ in the first syllable, and the noun is fixed in the plural here — singular auspice is a dictionary word almost nobody uses
entries.русский: под эгидой, под покровительством — кто поручился, а не кто выполнил работу
entries.register: formal; institutional, academic, diplomatic, and nonprofit prose — an American meets it in a press release, a conference program, a museum wall text, and a grant report
entries.type: complex (Latin auspicium, "the watching of birds," the taking of omens before a public act)
entries.complement: noun phrase naming an institution or a body, or a person acting in an institutional capacity — a university, an agency, a foundation, the United Nations. Never a gerund (✗ under the auspices of funding the work), never a finite clause. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: [event or work] [held / conducted / published] under the auspices of [sponsor] · Under the auspices of [sponsor], [clause]
entries.variants: under the aegis of — the same relation in Greek dress, after the shield of Athena, and a shade more literary. Under the umbrella of is the plain modern equivalent, under the banner of names a cause rather than a sponsor, and sponsored by is what a press release should usually say instead.
entries.contrast: It names the body whose sponsorship, protection, or formal authority the work was done under — and pointedly not the body that did the work. A survey conducted under the auspices of the National Academies tells you who vouched for it, not who wrote the questionnaire, and institutions like the phrase for exactly that reason. Against on behalf of: representing somebody is not the same as being backed by them. Against at the behest of: who ordered the work, against who lent it standing. Against plain by: by would claim the authorship this phrase is carefully not claiming. Against under color of: real authority against pretended authority.
entries.see also: at the behest of, on behalf of, courtesy of, under color of, by

entries.respell: by DINT uhv; weak /baɪ ˈdɪnt əv/, casually /baɪ ˈdɪnt ə/
entries.meaning: Attributes an achievement to effort or to a quality rather than to a tool. It always implies that the thing was hard and that the doer supplied whatever was missing out of their own resources.
examples: By dint of sheer persistence she got the sealed records released.
He made the roster by dint of being the only left-handed catcher in three counties.
The town got through the winter by dint of two generators and a great deal of goodwill.
She made partner by dint of long hours and an unnerving memory for names.
By dint of repetition alone, the slogan started to sound like common sense.
They kept the paper alive by dint of not paying themselves for two years.
entries.pronunciation note: by itself has no weak form and keeps its full /aɪ/
entries.русский: благодаря, ценой (усилий) — книжн.; о достигнутом упорством, а не инструментом
entries.register: formal, literary; faintly bookish
entries.complement: noun phrase — characteristically abstract (effort, persistence, sheer luck, brute force) — or a gerund (by dint of working nights). Never a finite clause, never a to-infinitive.
entries.pattern: [clause] by dint of [noun phrase / verb-ing] · By dint of [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: Narrower than by means of. By means of takes an instrument or a procedure; by dint of takes exertion, stubbornness, or a personal quality, and it says the result was forced out of an unwilling world. ✗ by dint of a crowbar is wrong where by dint of brute force is right. Dint is a fossil word meaning a blow, a stroke, and it survives in modern English only inside this phrase — which is why nobody can misuse the noun and everybody occasionally misspells it by dent of.
entries.see also: by means of, through, by virtue of, by

entries.respell: by MEENZ uhv; weak /baɪ ˈminz əv/, casually /baɪ ˈminz ə/
entries.meaning: Names the instrument, mechanism, or procedure that produced the result. Its whole value is unambiguity: in a sentence where with could be read as accompanied by, by means of cannot be.
examples: The two fractions were separated by means of a benchtop centrifuge.
Access to the vault is controlled by means of a keycard and a four-digit PIN.
The signal reaches the valley by means of a repeater on the ridge.
He supported the family by means of a night job and two lodgers.
Payment may be made by means of certified check or wire transfer.
The sample was purified by means of passing it twice through a silica column.
entries.русский: посредством, при помощи — офиц. и техн. указание на орудие или способ
entries.register: formal; technical, scientific, and legal writing
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (by means of dissolving the residue in acetone). Never a finite clause. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: [clause] by means of [noun phrase / verb-ing] · By means of [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: The long form of instrumental with and of method-marking by. Ordinary English says with a centrifuge; a patent application says by means of a centrifuge, because patent drafters want the instrument marked unmistakably and with has too many other jobs. Against by dint of: means versus effort. Against via: via is compact and can also mark a route, which by means of cannot. Against using: using is the modern technical-prose default and is shorter.
entries.see also: with, by, using, via, by dint of, by way of, by means of

entries.respell: by WAY uhv; weak /baɪ ˈweɪ əv/, casually /baɪ ˈweɪ ə/
examples: We drove home by way of Flagstaff to get around the storm.
Mail from the islands still comes by way of Miami.
The flight goes to Managua by way of Houston and adds four hours to the trip.
By way of apology he sent a bottle of wine and a note that explained nothing.
She mentioned the lawsuit only by way of introduction and then moved on.
He put up a slide of the 1954 map by way of showing how little had changed.
The money reaches the districts by way of a county trust.
He learned Portuguese by way of two years in São Paulo and a patient landlady.
Complaints get to the board by way of an ombudsman nobody has ever met.

senses.head: By the route of; passing through
examples: We drove home by way of Flagstaff to get around the storm.
Mail from the islands still comes by way of Miami.
The flight goes to Managua by way of Houston and adds four hours to the trip.

senses.head: As a form of; for the purpose of
body: Takes a bare noun with no article, or a gerund.
examples: By way of apology he sent a bottle of wine and a note that explained nothing.
She mentioned the lawsuit only by way of introduction and then moved on.
He put up a slide of the 1954 map by way of showing how little had changed.

senses.head: Through the mechanism of; by means of
examples: The money reaches the districts by way of a county trust.
He learned Portuguese by way of two years in São Paulo and a patient landlady.
Complaints get to the board by way of an ombudsman nobody has ever met.

entries.русский: через (транзитом); в качестве (извинения, примера); посредством чего-л.
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: noun phrase; a gerund (by way of explaining himself); or — in the manner sense only — a bare article-less abstract noun: by way of apology, by way of introduction, by way of illustration. Never a finite clause of any kind, and never a to-infinitive: ✗ by way of to explain.
entries.pattern: [clause] by way of [place] (route) · [clause] by way of [bare abstract noun] (purpose) · [clause] by way of [noun phrase] (means)
entries.contrast: Three jobs share one phrase and the complement tells you which is running. A place name means route and equals via. A bare abstract noun means as a form of and equals as or as a kind of. Anything else means means and equals by means of, which is the weakest of the three uses and usually cuttable — by way of illustration is just for example. Compare the reference-and-topic use at by way of.
entries.see also: via, through, by means of, out of, by way of, by way of

examples: He built the whole shed out of salvaged barn siding.
The bowl is turned out of a single piece of walnut.
She made supper out of whatever was left in the pantry.
Nine out of ten of the households surveyed had never heard of the program.
She scored ninety-two out of a hundred and was furious about the eight.
Three out of the four bridges on that stretch are rated structurally deficient.
The overtime came out of the general fund, not out of the grant.
Two of the positions are paid out of federal money that runs out in June.
He covered the difference out of his own pocket, which is the line the auditors underlined.

senses.head: The material a thing was made from
body: The stuff is still recognizable in the product.
examples: He built the whole shed out of salvaged barn siding.
The bowl is turned out of a single piece of walnut.
She made supper out of whatever was left in the pantry.

senses.head: Out of a stated set — the proportion sense
body: Both numbers are given, and the second is the whole.
examples: Nine out of ten of the households surveyed had never heard of the program.
She scored ninety-two out of a hundred and was furious about the eight.
Three out of the four bridges on that stretch are rated structurally deficient.

senses.head: The fund or source a cost was paid from
examples: The overtime came out of the general fund, not out of the grant.
Two of the positions are paid out of federal money that runs out in June.
He covered the difference out of his own pocket, which is the line the auditors underlined.

entries.pronunciation note: OWT uhv; weak /ˈaʊt əv/ and, at any ordinary speed, the two words run together as /ˈaʊtə/ — OW-tuh — which is what the eye-spelling outta is transcribing, and the reason learners write ✗ out a curiosity
entries.русский: из (материала); из (общего числа): nine out of ten; за счёт (средств, фонда)
entries.register: neutral; one of the highest-frequency prepositions in the language
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or a fused relative (built out of what was left in the barn). A gerund occurs only in the motive sense treated elsewhere (out of not wanting to embarrass her), and even there it grates. Never a finite clause and never a that-clause — ✗ out of that he was tired. It strands as a unit, both words together: What is it made out of?, the fund the raise came out of — but the of can never be dropped and never left behind: ✗ what is it made out?
entries.pattern: [verb of making] out of [material] · [number] out of [number] · [cost or payment] out of [fund or source]
entries.contrast: This entry owns the material, proportion, and funding-source senses. The spatial sense (out of the building) is at out of, the motive sense (out of spite, out of curiosity) at out of, and the general all-senses entry at out of. Against of for materials: made of oak names the substance and leaves the substance recognizable; made out of oak insists that raw stuff was transformed — which is why a table made out of a door is idiomatic and ✗ a table made of a door is not. Against from: from is the marker when the material is no longer visible in the product (wine from grapes, paper from rags), out of when it still is. Against in for proportions: one in five households is a rate over a population, nine out of ten dentists is a count taken from a stated set — which is why a test score is always 92 out of 100 and never ✗ 92 in 100. Out alone is an adverb and a verb particle (She went out, Cross it out, The fire is out) and takes no object at all, which is the test; the preposition is the two-word form.
entries.see also: of, from, in, by means of, via, out of (movement), out of (cause), out of (complex)

examples: He built the business through twenty years of eighteen-hour days.
Most of our hiring happens through referrals rather than postings.
She got her start through working weekends at a station nobody listened to.
She got the loan through a credit union rather than a bank.
You can only reach him through his agent, and his agent does not return calls.
The house sold through a broker who never once set foot in it.
The mix-up happened through a clerical error, not through malice.
Through no fault of her own she ended up in the wrong terminal in the wrong city.
Two boxes of personnel records were lost through sheer inattention.

senses.head: By the means or method of
body: The process that produced the result.
examples: He built the business through twenty years of eighteen-hour days.
Most of our hiring happens through referrals rather than postings.
She got her start through working weekends at a station nobody listened to.

senses.head: Through the agency of; via an intermediary
examples: She got the loan through a credit union rather than a bank.
You can only reach him through his agent, and his agent does not return calls.
The house sold through a broker who never once set foot in it.

senses.head: Because of — normally with a fault, an accident, or a lack
examples: The mix-up happened through a clerical error, not through malice.
Through no fault of her own she ended up in the wrong terminal in the wrong city.
Two boxes of personnel records were lost through sheer inattention.

entries.pronunciation note: no true weak form; in rapid speech the vowel shortens toward /θrʊ/ and, before a consonant, as far as /θrə/ (through the door /θrə ðə ˈdɔr/). The spelling thru is signage and shorthand, not standard prose.
entries.русский: благодаря, посредством; через посредника; из-за (оплошности, недосмотра)
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund (through working weekends for two years). Never a finite clause. It strands freely: the agency I found it through, Who did you hear it through?
entries.pattern: [clause] through [noun phrase / verb-ing] · Through [noun phrase], [clause] · stranded: the program I got the job through
entries.contrast: This entry covers the means and intermediary senses; the spatial sense (through the tunnel) is at through, the inclusive-date sense (Monday through Friday) is at through, and the fault-and-failing sense sketched in sense 3 below is worked out in full at through. Against by: by marks the direct agent or the medium, through marks the channel that carried it — I heard it by phone is the medium, I heard it through a friend is the intermediary. Against via: near-synonyms for the intermediary sense, but through takes gerunds and strands where via does neither. Also an adverb and a particle — Let me through, We got through, I'm through with him — and there it has no object at all, which is the test.
entries.see also: by, via, by means of, by way of, through (movement), through (time), through (cause)

entries.meaning: Names the tool, material, or resource an agent employed. It is the plainest instrumental marker English has after with, and unlike with it says nothing about accompaniment, possession, or manner.
examples: Tighten the bracket using a ten-millimeter socket.
The map was drawn using satellite imagery from 2019.
She paid using a card she had reported stolen the week before.
Using nothing but a paperclip, he got the battery cover off.
We track attendance using a shared spreadsheet nobody has permission to edit.
The team modeled the outbreak using three separate sets of assumptions.
entries.pronunciation note: no weak form — it keeps its own stress, which is one sign it is still half a verb
entries.русский: используя, с помощью — называет инструмент; деепричастие, ставшее предлогом
entries.register: neutral; the default in technical writing and instructions
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun. Never a finite clause, and — unlike a true preposition — it does not take a gerund: ✗ using boiling the water. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: [clause] using [noun phrase] · Using [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: A present participle that has drifted most of the way into prepositionhood. It competes with instrumental with and formal by means of, and technical prose prefers it because it names a tool without any of with's other meanings: Open the file with Sarah is ambiguous, Open the file using Sarah's account is not. Its participial origin still shows: when the main clause has no plausible user, you get a dangling modifier — ✗ Using a spreadsheet, the numbers were checked says the numbers used the spreadsheet. Compare given and considering, which have gone further and no longer need a subject to attach to.
entries.see also: with, by means of, with the aid of, given, considering

examples: Send the signed copy via email; the original can follow by mail.
Tickets are available only via the mobile app, which is the whole complaint.
Updates go out via text message and a recorded call.
The story reached us via a stringer in Ankara.
Payments clear via the ACH network, usually in two business days.
He got the interview via a former roommate who owed him a favor.

senses.head: By way of a medium or channel of transmission
examples: Send the signed copy via email; the original can follow by mail.
Tickets are available only via the mobile app, which is the whole complaint.
Updates go out via text message and a recorded call.

senses.head: Through an intermediary — a person, an agency, a system
examples: The story reached us via a stringer in Ankara.
Payments clear via the ACH network, usually in two business days.
He got the interview via a former roommate who owed him a favor.

entries.pronunciation note: VEE-uh — the second is commoner in British English and in Latin tags. No weak form: it carries a stress of its own, which is part of why it feels crisper than by way of.
entries.русский: через, посредством — о канале передачи или о посреднике
entries.register: neutral to formal; very common in technical and business prose
entries.type: simple (Latin via, the ablative of via "road")
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun. Never a gerund and never a finite clause — ✗ via sending an email, ✗ via he told me. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: [clause] via [noun phrase] · [destination] via [waypoint] · [noun phrase] via [medium]
entries.contrast: The travel-route sense is at via; this entry is the medium and intermediary sense. Against by for media: both work, but by wants a bare article-less noun (by email, by phone, by the app) while via takes either (via email, via the app). Against through: identical in meaning for intermediaries, but through takes gerunds and strands and via does neither — ✗ the single commonest error with this word is putting an -ing form after it. Against by means of: via is the compact modern equivalent and has almost displaced it outside legal drafting.
entries.see also: through, by, by means of, by way of, via

entries.meaning: Marks an instrument or a helper that made an already-difficult thing possible. The agent stays firmly in the sentence's subject position; the aid is subordinate, which is exactly the difference from by.
examples: The worn inscription was finally read with the aid of raking light.
She walks now with the aid of a cane and a great deal of stubbornness.
With the help of two neighbors, they got the tree off the driveway before dark.
The bill passed with the assistance of four members of the other party.
He finished the manuscript with the aid of a small grant and a very patient editor.
Divers recovered the recorder with the aid of a remotely operated vehicle.
entries.pronunciation note: with thee AYD uhv; weak /wəθ ði ˈeɪd əv/, casually /wəθ ði ˈeɪd ə/ — with reduces to /wəθ/ and the of to bare /ə/, so the whole phrase can come out as three unstressed syllables around aid
entries.русский: с помощью, при помощи — книжн.; подразумевает преодолённую трудность
entries.register: formal
entries.complement: noun phrase — an instrument or a person. A gerund is possible but rare and clumsy. Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] with the aid of [noun phrase] · With the aid of [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.variants: with the help of — the everyday form and the commoner of the two in American English, and the only comfortable choice when the complement is a person. With the assistance of — the most formal, standard in official and academic prose.
entries.contrast: Against plain instrumental with: He read the inscription with a magnifying glass and with the aid of a magnifying glass mean the same thing, but the long form implies a difficulty that had to be overcome. Against by means of: by means of is neutral about difficulty and treats the instrument as sufficient; with the aid of treats it as assistance to an agent who was already working at it. Against using: using is neutral and modern, with the aid of is formal and slightly effortful.
entries.see also: with, using, by means of, thanks to, courtesy of

entries.meaning: Says that something is done in the recognizable style of a named model. The name is doing the definitional work, so it has to be a name the reader already carries around — this is a preposition that fails completely on an unfamiliar complement.
examples: He gave a rambling hour-long press conference à la his predecessor.
The episode ends on a freeze-frame à la every sitcom made between 1979 and 1988.
She writes long comma-spliced paragraphs à la Kerouac and edits none of them.
They want a walkable downtown à la Portland, on a third of Portland's budget.
The team plays a switch-everything defense à la the 2015 Warriors.
He does the whole deadpan-narrator thing à la Wes Anderson.
entries.русский: в стиле, на манер кого-л. — с оттенком подражания, оммажа или пародии
entries.register: neutral to journalistic; knowing in tone
entries.type: complex (French à la manière de, clipped)
entries.complement: noun phrase, characteristically a proper name — a person, a work, a brand, a place, an era. Never a gerund, never a finite clause. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: [clause] à la [proper name] · [noun phrase] à la [proper name]
entries.variants: written a la without the accent in a great deal of American copy; à la is the careful spelling and the one dictionaries head. The French gender agreement does not survive: it is à la before every complement, masculine or not.
entries.contrast: A compact in the style of. Against like: like compares anything to anything and asserts nothing about intent, while à la compares a way of doing to a known model and always carries a whiff of imitation, homage, or parody. Against after the manner of: the same meaning at the opposite register — à la is light and current, after the manner of is heavy and belongs in a museum label. Do not confuse the preposition with the frozen culinary nouns à la carte, à la mode, à la king, which take no complement at all.
entries.see also: like, after the manner of, as, in the manner of

examples: According to the medical examiner, the death was accidental.
Turnout was up nine points, according to preliminary county figures.
According to whoever answered the phone at the clerk's office, the filing window closes at noon.
Everything went according to plan until about the second hour.
Assemble the shelves according to the diagram on page four, not the one on the box.
Members are seated according to seniority, which takes longer than the vote does.
Rates change according to how much water you use.
Class size is set according to the age of the students.
The bonus is prorated according to what each office billed in the fourth quarter.

senses.head: On the authority of; as reported by
body: The source is somebody other than the writer.
examples: According to the medical examiner, the death was accidental.
Turnout was up nine points, according to preliminary county figures.
According to whoever answered the phone at the clerk's office, the filing window closes at noon.

senses.head: In conformity with; in the manner prescribed by
examples: Everything went according to plan until about the second hour.
Assemble the shelves according to the diagram on page four, not the one on the box.
Members are seated according to seniority, which takes longer than the vote does.

senses.head: In proportion to; varying with
examples: Rates change according to how much water you use.
Class size is set according to the age of the students.
The bonus is prorated according to what each office billed in the fourth quarter.

entries.русский: по словам кого-л. (со ссылкой на источник); согласно чему-л.; в зависимости от
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: complex (participial in origin, from the verb accord)
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or a wh-nominal — either a fused relative (according to what the manual says, according to whoever answered the phone) or an embedded interrogative (according to how much water you use, according to which shift you are on). Never a that-clause, never any other finite clause, and never a gerund — ✗ according to he said, ✗ according to that the manual says, ✗ according to reading the file. The to here is a preposition and not the infinitive marker, so a bare infinitive is impossible too: ✗ according to conserve water. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: According to [source], [clause] · [clause], according to [source] · [clause] according to [standard or plan]
entries.contrast: Two distinct jobs, and this file owns the second and third. As an evidential (according to the mayor) it reports someone else's claim and quietly declines to endorse it — which is why ✗ according to me is odd and why attaching it to an obvious fact (according to the calendar, today is Tuesday) reads as sarcasm. As a manner preposition (according to plan, according to the rules) it means in conformity with and equals in accordance with and in keeping with. The general entry is at according to; as per is the business-memo version of the conformity sense.
entries.see also: according to, as per, per, in accordance with, in keeping with

entries.meaning: Says that the thing was made or done in conscious imitation of a named model's method. Where à la is a quick comparison, this is a claim about how the work was actually made.
examples: He wrote a sequence of unrhymed sonnets after the manner of Berryman.
The chapel was decorated in the manner of the Venetian churches he had spent two years studying.
She argued the case after the manner of a prosecutor rather than a defense attorney.
The label read simply "Landscape with Cattle, after Cuyp."
The house rambles in the manner of a New England farmhouse that grew by accretion.
The score is orchestrated after the manner of the late Romantics, down to the doubled horns.
entries.pronunciation note: AF-ter thuh MAN-er uhv; weak /ˈæftɚ ðə ˈmænɚ əv/, casually /ˈæftɚ ðə ˈmænɚ ə/ — five syllables of which only two are stressed, which is most of why the phrase feels heavy
entries.русский: в манере, по образцу — книжн., искусствовед.; об осознанном подражании
entries.register: formal, literary; standard in art criticism and museum cataloguing
entries.complement: noun phrase, typically a proper name, a named school, or a period. Never a gerund, never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] after the manner of [model] · [noun phrase] after the manner of [model]
entries.variants: in the manner of — commoner in American English and the form to prefer in ordinary prose; it has its own entry at in the manner of. In the style of is the plainest member of the family and the one to use when no art-world echo is wanted. Bare after in museum and auction cataloguing (After Cuyp) is a term of art, not a casual clipping: it means a later copy by another hand.
entries.contrast: The formal counterpart of à la and of manner like. Against like: like asserts resemblance, after the manner of asserts deliberate imitation of a method. In cataloguing the terms are graded and legally meaningful: by is autograph, attributed to is probably autograph, studio of means the workshop produced it, in the manner of means a follower whose hand is unknown, and after means somebody else copied it later. Using them loosely in a sale description is a misrepresentation, not a style choice.
entries.see also: à la, like, as, in the guise of, in the manner of

entries.meaning: States that something conforms to an instruction, a document, or an established practice. It is pure register: it signals that the writer is operating inside a bureaucracy and is covering themselves.
examples: The deposit was refunded as per the terms of the lease.
As per your request, I have attached last quarter's figures.
Invoices are due within thirty days as per company policy.
The units were installed as per the manufacturer's instructions.
He turned up forty minutes late, as per usual.
Access was revoked as per the offboarding checklist.
entries.русский: согласно, в соответствии с — канцелярит; as per usual — шутл. «как водится»
entries.register: business and bureaucratic; disliked by every usage authority that mentions it
entries.complement: noun phrase only — almost always a document, an instruction, or a prior communication (as per your email, as per the contract). Never a gerund, never a wh-nominal, never a finite clause: ✗ as per you asked → as per your request, or better still as you asked.
entries.pattern: As per [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] as per [noun phrase] · fixed: as per usual
entries.contrast: A redundant compound: per already means according to, so the as adds nothing, and commentators have been calling the phrase illiterate since the 1800s. It survives because it sounds official. In plain prose write per, according to, following, or nothing at all — as per our conversation is as we discussed. Note that as per usual is a separate jokey idiom that is meant to sound wrong, and it is the one use nobody objects to. Do not confuse it with distributive per (sixty miles per hour), which is a different job and perfectly respectable. Its life as a document-naming phrase is treated with the prepositions of reference at as per.
entries.see also: per, according to, in accordance with, pursuant to, as per (reference)

examples: He drives like a man who has never been ticketed in his life.
The fabric feels like raw silk and costs about a tenth as much.
Standing there in the doorway, she sounded exactly like her mother.
He was shaking like a leaf and pretending he was cold.
It is just like him to volunteer for a committee and then miss every meeting.
That is not like her at all — she is never late.
It would be just like the county to repave the street the week after the parade.
Bring something small: a paperback, a deck of cards, something like that.
Cities like Tucson and El Paso have been planning for this for twenty years.
We want something like what they built in Boise, only smaller.
The whole repair came to like four hundred dollars.
We waited like twenty minutes and then just left.
What is the new place like?
I have not met him. What is he like?
It looks like rain before noon.
That sounds like a plan nobody has thought through.

senses.head: Resembling; in the manner of
examples: He drives like a man who has never been ticketed in his life.
The fabric feels like raw silk and costs about a tenth as much.
Standing there in the doorway, she sounded exactly like her mother.
He was shaking like a leaf and pretending he was cold.

senses.head: Characteristic of; typical of
body: Almost always with be, and very often negated.
examples: It is just like him to volunteer for a committee and then miss every meeting.
That is not like her at all — she is never late.
It would be just like the county to repave the street the week after the parade.

senses.head: Introducing an example
examples: Bring something small: a paperback, a deck of cards, something like that.
Cities like Tucson and El Paso have been planning for this for twenty years.
We want something like what they built in Boise, only smaller.

senses.head: Approximately — informal, spoken
examples: The whole repair came to like four hundred dollars.
We waited like twenty minutes and then just left.

senses.head: In the fixed question What is X like?
examples: What is the new place like?
I have not met him. What is he like?

senses.head: Apparently, seemingly — after look, sound, feel, seem, smell, taste
examples: It looks like rain before noon.
That sounds like a plan nobody has thought through.

entries.pronunciation note: a full lexical word with no reduced form, though it is routinely unstressed
entries.русский: как, подобно — сравнение; свойственно кому-л.; например; разг. «примерно»
entries.register: neutral as a preposition; the conjunction use (like I said) is informal, and the approximative use is informal
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun (like me, like her and me — ✗ like I, ✗ like she), a gerund (It's like flying), or a fused relative (like what happened in 2019, like whoever ran it last year). As a preposition it cannot take a finite clause, and never a that-clause. Like I said and like he does are the conjunction like, which is standard in American speech and casual writing and is still edited out of formal prose in favor of as. It strands only in the fixed interrogative What is she like?
entries.pattern: [verb] like [noun phrase] · [be] like [noun phrase] · like [verb-ing] · Like [noun phrase], [clause] · fixed: What is X like?
entries.contrast: ✗ Against as, the classic split. Like takes a noun and asserts resemblance; as takes a clause, or a role actually held — She works like a lawyer means she resembles one, She works as a lawyer means she is one; see as. The three-way ladder is worth memorizing: Do it like me (imitate my example, everywhere), Do it as I do (formal writing), Do it like I do (standard American speech, flagged in formal writing). For introducing examples, such as is the conservative choice in edited prose because like can be read as resembling — poets like Frost may or may not include Frost — though the distinction is not observed in general American usage, where like introduces examples freely. ✗ Also a verb (I like it), a noun (and the like), an adjective (of like mind), an adverb, a conjunction (like I said), a suffix (childlike), a quotative (he was like, no way), and a discourse particle — the preposition is the one with a noun-phrase object and no clause after it. The comparison entry, with the case and parallelism rules in full, is at like.
entries.see also: as, unlike, à la, after the manner of, with, like (comparison), such as

entries.meaning: Names the thing that hid the act. Whatever follows it is doing double duty: it is both the circumstance the act took place in and the screen that kept the act from being seen — which is why the phrase always implies that somebody meant not to be noticed.
examples: The battalion crossed the river under cover of darkness and a heavy river fog.
They moved the equipment out under cover of night, two trucks at a time.
The engineers repaired the bridge under cover of an artillery barrage.
The transfers were made under cover of a routine reorganization.
Under cover of anonymity, half the department said what it actually thought.
He solicited the donations under cover of a charity that had stopped operating years before.

senses.head: Concealed or screened by
examples: The battalion crossed the river under cover of darkness and a heavy river fog.
They moved the equipment out under cover of night, two trucks at a time.
The engineers repaired the bridge under cover of an artillery barrage.

senses.head: Using something as a screen or a pretext
examples: The transfers were made under cover of a routine reorganization.
Under cover of anonymity, half the department said what it actually thought.
He solicited the donations under cover of a charity that had stopped operating years before.

entries.pronunciation note: UHN-der KUV-er uhv; weak /ˈʌndɚ ˈkʌvɚ əv/, casually /ˈʌndɚ ˈkʌvɚ ə/ — neither under nor cover reduces, so the whole weakening falls on the of, which is why the phrase is so often heard as under cover-uh darkness
entries.русский: под покровом (темноты), под прикрытием — о том, что скрыло действие
entries.register: neutral to formal; military history, journalism, and narrative prose. The collocation under cover of darkness is all but fixed and is the form most readers have met.
entries.complement: noun phrase naming whatever supplies the concealment or the pretext — darkness, night, fog, a barrage, anonymity, a reorganization. Normally with no article: under cover of darkness, not ✗ under cover of the darkness. Never a gerund (✗ under cover of getting dark), never a finite clause. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: [clause] under cover of [concealment] · Under cover of [concealment], [clause]
entries.variants: under the cover of is attested and reads a shade more literal; American editors keep the article-less form in the fixed phrase. Written solid, undercover is an adjective and an adverb (an undercover officer, she worked undercover) and takes no object at all — which is the test that separates it from this preposition.
entries.contrast: Against under color of, the phrase it is constantly confused with: under color of is legal and means under the pretended authority of — acting under color of state law is the operative language in federal civil rights suits — while under cover of means hidden behind something. Against during: during the night names when it happened, under cover of night names the night as the thing being used to hide, so only the second implies a purpose. Against in the guise of: a guise is an appearance put on, a cover is a screen hidden behind. Against on the pretext of: the pretext is the stated reason, the cover is the concealment it buys.
entries.see also: under color of, in the guise of, on the pretext of, during, under

Her handwriting is completely unlike his, which is how the forgery was caught.

senses.head: In contrast to
examples: Unlike her sister, she never learned to swim.

senses.head: Not characteristic of; not resembling
