entries.pronunciation note: stressed on the second syllable, and no weak form
entries.русский: в отличие от — противопоставление; предикативно — «не похоже на кого-л.», «не в его духе»
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: compound (un- + like, no longer analyzed as two pieces) — also an adjective (two unlike quantities, unlike poles attract), where it takes no object
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun (unlike me), a gerund (Unlike renting, buying builds equity), or a fused relative (unlike what I said last week). Never a finite clause — ✗ unlike I said; the repairs are unlike what I said or a contrastive conjunction such as whereas. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: Unlike [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause], unlike [noun phrase] · [be] unlike [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The negation of prepositional like, with two readings that split by position. Sentence-initial it sets up a contrast between two things filling the same role — and the two must be genuinely comparable or the sentence dangles: ✗ Unlike most cities, Houston's zoning is minimal compares cities to zoning; write Unlike most cities, Houston has almost no zoning. Predicatively (That's unlike him) it means uncharacteristic, matching sense 2 of like. It is not the verb dislike, and it is not quite not like: He is not like his father denies resemblance in general, while Unlike his father, he… asserts a contrast on one named point. The litotes not unlike is a hedge meaning somewhat similar to. For the adjectival rival, American English writes different from, and different than before a clause; British different to does not belong in American copy — see different from. The full comparison entry is at unlike.
entries.see also: like, as, other than, in contrast to, unlike (comparison), different from

entries.meaning: Distributes a quantity over a unit. It is the most frequent rate marker in spoken American English by a wide margin, and it is invisible to most speakers, who take it for the article.
examples: She takes the medication twice a day with food.
Ground chuck was four dollars a pound that week.
He drives about eighty miles an hour on the interstate, which explains the three tickets.
Tickets were fifteen dollars a head at the door and twelve in advance.
The plant turns out two thousand units a week on one shift.
We were getting maybe three calls an hour by the end of the night.
entries.pronunciation note: uh — the weak form is the normal one here
entries.русский: распределительное «в», «за»: twice a day — дважды в день; это не артикль, а значение «per»
entries.register: neutral; the everyday spoken form
entries.complement: a bare singular count noun of time, quantity, or measure: a day, a week, a head, a pound, a gallon, a person, a mile. Never a plural (✗ twice a days), never a gerund, never a clause. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: [frequency] a [unit] · [price] a [unit] · [quantity] a [unit]
entries.variants: an before a vowel sound (an hour, an ounce, an acre). per is the formal and technical equivalent; the replaces it inside the by construction (by the hour).
entries.contrast: This is not the indefinite article, even though it is spelled and pronounced identically. It descends from Old English on worn down to nothing — the same erosion that produced nowadays, asleep, ashore — and it means per. The test is substitution: twice a day is twice per day, never twice one day. Against per: identical in meaning, opposite in register — sixty miles an hour on the road, 60 miles per hour on the spec sheet. Do not mix the two: ✗ per an hour. British English uses this form somewhat more freely in prices (two pounds a kilo); American English is comfortable with either.
entries.see also: per, by, at, at the rate of

entries.meaning: Says that one quantity is determined by another and moves with it. The claim is about dependence only — not about direction, not about shape, and not about cause — which is exactly why the sciences want it and why it goes slack when it is borrowed for prose that means because of.
examples: Plot the reaction rate as a function of temperature and the curve will make the argument for you.
Fuel burn rises steeply as a function of speed above about forty knots.
The model estimates dropout as a function of class size, commute time, and hours worked.
Premiums are set as a function of age, zip code, and claims history.
Signal loss increases as a function of the square of the distance.
Turnout in these precincts moves almost entirely as a function of how close the race looks in the last week.
entries.pronunciation note: az uh FUNK-shun uhv; weak /əz ə ˈfʌŋkʃən əv/, casually /əz ə ˈfʌŋkʃn ə/ — five syllables carrying one real stress, on funk-
entries.русский: в зависимости от — научн.; одна величина определяется другой
entries.register: formal; the standard phrasing in mathematics, the sciences, engineering, and economics, and a vogue phrase everywhere else
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a variable — something that can take different values (temperature, dose, income, distance, time) — or a wh-nominal standing in for one (as a function of how far you live from the plant, as a function of what the market did that week). Never a gerund: ✗ as a function of raising the dose → as a function of dose. When an -ing word does turn up it is an adjective on the variable (as a function of increasing temperature), not a complement of the preposition. Never a finite clause: ✗ as a function of the temperature rose. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: [quantity] varies as a function of [variable] · plot [y] as a function of [x] · [clause] as a function of [variable]
entries.variants: predicative a function of with no as — the delay is a function of two things — is the same metaphor used as a noun phrase after be, and it is the commoner shape in business prose.
entries.contrast: In its home fields it claims a real dependence, y = f(x), and it also fixes the axes: plot pressure as a function of volume puts volume along the bottom and pressure up the side. In general prose it has thinned into a dressed-up because of — the decision was made as a function of politics is made for political reasons — and that is the use to cut. Against in proportion to: proportionality is one particular function, a straight line through the origin, so pay rises in proportion to hours is a far stronger claim than pay rises as a function of hours. Against according to sense 3 and depending on: the ordinary-language equivalents, and the right choice when no mathematics is involved.
entries.see also: in proportion to, according to, by a factor of, depending on, per

entries.meaning: Introduces an explicit ratio of quantity to unit. It is the register-marked version of what at, a, and per do more briefly, and it earns its length only when the ratio itself is the point of the sentence.
examples: The loan accrues interest at the rate of six percent a year, compounded monthly.
Water was coming into the hold at a rate of about forty gallons a minute.
Overtime is paid at the rate of one and a half times the base wage.
The glacier has been retreating at a rate of roughly thirty feet a year since 1998.
Bonds were redeemed at the rate of a hundred dollars on the thousand.
The state reimburses mileage at the rate of sixty-seven cents a mile.
entries.pronunciation note: at thuh RAYT uhv; weak /ət ðə ˈreɪt əv/, casually /ət ðə ˈreɪt ə/
entries.русский: из расчёта, по ставке — офиц.; вводит явное соотношение количества к единице
entries.register: formal; standard in finance, contracts, and technical reporting
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a quantity — a number, a sum, a percentage, or a whole ratio phrase. Never a gerund, never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] at the rate of [quantity] per [unit] · [clause] at a rate of [percentage]
entries.variants: at a rate of — used when the rate is being introduced rather than pointed back to. Both are standard American English and the choice is the ordinary a/the choice.
entries.contrast: The explicit form of rate-marking at, which is what plain prose uses: at 6 percent rather than at a rate of 6 percent. Against per: per names the unit, at the rate of frames the whole ratio, and the two normally appear in the same phrase. Do not confuse it with the idiom at this rate / at that rate, which takes no of and means if things keep going the way they are going.
entries.see also: per, a, at, by

entries.meaning: States how many times larger or smaller something got. It is the compact way to report a change whose size is better described as a multiple than as a difference, which is most changes that run over an order of magnitude.
examples: Processing time dropped by a factor of four once the job moved off the old server.
The new assay is more sensitive by a factor of about a thousand.
Demand rose by a factor of three in the two weeks after the recall.
The first estimate was off by a factor of ten, and nobody caught it until the model was rerun.
Adding the second filter cut particulate counts by a factor of six.
Legal costs have grown by a factor of five since the first suit was filed.
entries.pronunciation note: by uh FAK-ter uhv; weak /baɪ ə ˈfæktɚ əv/, casually /baɪ ə ˈfæktɚ ə/ — by keeps its full /aɪ/ and takes no weak form
entries.русский: в … раз — во сколько раз что-то выросло или уменьшилось
entries.register: neutral to formal; scientific, technical, financial, and journalistic
entries.complement: a number or a numeric expression — two, ten, a thousand, 2.5, three or four. Never a gerund, never a finite clause, and never a bare noun of quantity: ✗ by a factor of the population, ✗ by a factor of money. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: [verb of increase or decrease] by a factor of [number] · [comparative] by a factor of [number] · off by a factor of [number]
entries.contrast: The multiplicative twin of additive by: the budget went up by two million adds, the budget went up by a factor of two doubles. Two errors are worth learning around. Downward: reduced by a factor of ten means divided by ten, down to a tenth — and reduced by ten times, which is what people reach for instead, is not English arithmetic. Percentages: increased by a factor of two is an increase of a hundred percent, so ✗ increased by a factor of 50 percent is a category error, and any change smaller than a doubling wants a percentage instead. Against times: times multiplies two named numbers (seven times eight), by a factor of names the multiplier of a change. Against to the power of: multiplying against exponentiating.
entries.see also: times, to the power of, by, at the rate of, as a function of

entries.meaning: Divides and keeps only what is left over. The arithmetic sense is the operation every clock, calendar, and check digit runs on; the extended sense borrows the same move for an argument, sweeping a remainder of small problems aside so that the main claim can go through.
examples: Seventeen modulo five is two.
Hours on a clock are counted mod twelve, which is why four hours after ten is two.
The check digit is the running total modulo eleven.
Two integers are congruent mod nine when they leave the same remainder.
Modulo a few typos, the proof goes through exactly as written.
The design is finished modulo deciding what to do about the cache.
Their numbers agree with ours modulo the difference in sample frames.

senses.head: In modular arithmetic: with the remainder after division by
examples: Seventeen modulo five is two.
Hours on a clock are counted mod twelve, which is why four hours after ten is two.
The check digit is the running total modulo eleven.
Two integers are congruent mod nine when they leave the same remainder.

senses.head: Except for; setting aside
examples: Modulo a few typos, the proof goes through exactly as written.
The design is finished modulo deciding what to do about the cache.
Their numbers agree with ours modulo the difference in sample frames.

entries.pronunciation note: MAH-dyuh-loh. No weak form — it keeps its own stress. The clipped form mod is /mɑd/ · MAHD, and it is what almost everyone actually says.
entries.русский: по модулю (остаток от деления); жарг. — «не считая», «если отбросить»
entries.register: technical and neutral inside mathematics and computing; academic and programmer jargon in the extended sense, where outside a seminar room or an engineering channel it reads as showing off. Not general American English.
entries.type: simple (Latin, the ablative of modulus, "a small measure")
entries.complement: in the arithmetic sense a number or numeric expression (17 modulo 5, mod 2π, mod n); in the extended sense a noun phrase naming what is being set aside (modulo a few typos) or a gerund (modulo fixing the tests first). Never a finite clause. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: [number] modulo [number] · [number] and [number] are congruent (mod [modulus]) · [claim] modulo [caveat]
entries.variants: clipped mod is the normal form in speech, in writing, and in code, and the parenthetical (mod n) is the standard notation in a congruence. The operator is written % in C, Java, Python, and JavaScript, mod in Pascal and SQL, and %% in R.
entries.contrast: Sense 1 discards the quotient and keeps the remainder, which is what makes it the clock-and-calendar operator: hours run modulo 12, weekdays modulo 7. Sense 2 is the extension mathematicians made and programmers borrowed — modulo the caveats above, the result holds means setting those aside — which puts it in the family of except for, apart from, and leaving aside, only in a much narrower register. Against per: both are Latin and both divide, but per distributes a quantity over a unit while modulo throws the quotient away. One trap worth knowing if you write code: the mathematician's mod is never negative, but the % operator in C and Java is — -7 % 3 is -1 there and 2 in Python.
entries.see also: per, times, over, except for, apart from

examples: The room is two hundred dollars per night, plus tax and a resort fee nobody explains.
Output is measured in barrels per day.
The state spends about twelve thousand dollars per student.
Income per capita has been essentially flat for a decade.

Per our agreement, the deposit is nonrefundable after Friday.

examples: The room is two hundred dollars per night, plus tax and a resort fee nobody explains.

Income per capita has been essentially flat for a decade.

senses.head: According to; in accordance with
examples: Per our agreement, the deposit is nonrefundable after Friday.
The forms were filed per the court's instructions.

body: Surviving mainly in commercial and legal formulas.
examples: The goods were shipped per the SS Marquette out of New Orleans.
Notice may be given per certified mail or per hand delivery.
Payment was remitted per the escrow agent named in Schedule B.

entries.pronunciation note: pur — the weak form is the normal one, and the vowel is r-colored either way, so the unstressed form rhymes with the second syllable of water: sixty miles per hour is /ˈsɪksti ˈmaɪlz pɚ ˈaʊɚ/
entries.русский: за, на (единицу): per hour; согласно (документу) — деловой стиль; устар. посредством
entries.register: formal, technical, and commercial in the rate sense; the according to sense is business jargon
entries.complement: in the rate sense, a bare singular noun with no determiner: per hour, per person, per capita, per unit — ✗ per an hour, ✗ per the hour. In the according to sense it does take a determiner (per our agreement, per the memo). Never a gerund, never a finite clause. It can stand postpositively with the unit understood: forty dollars per.
entries.pattern: [quantity] per [bare unit] · [quantity] per (unit understood) · Per [document], [clause]
entries.contrast: Against a: identical in the rate sense, different only in register. Against for: four dollars per pound is a rate, four dollars for a pound is one transaction. Against as per: as per is this word with a useless as bolted on, and usage guides that tolerate per your email still object to as per your email. Watch the Latin fossils, which keep the article-less rule: per annum, per capita, per diem, per se, per stirpes, and per cent — written as one word, percent, in American English and as two in British.
entries.see also: a, at the rate of, as per, according to, by

senses.head: Expressing a multiple or a ratio

entries.pronunciation note: a full lexical word with no weak form; it keeps its own stress even between two stressed numerals (seven TIMES eight)
entries.русский: умножить на; во столько-то раз: seven times eight — семью восемь
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: simple (a plural noun reanalyzed as a preposition) — also the ordinary plural noun (three times a week, at times, the good times), which takes no complement
entries.complement: noun phrase — a number, a quantity, a measure noun, or a fused relative (three times what they paid). Never a gerund, never a finite clause. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: [number] times [number] · [number] times [the] [noun phrase] · [number] times [comparative adjective] · [number] times as [adjective] as [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: As a preposition it is the spoken form of the multiplication sign, and the phrase it heads is singular: Six times four is twenty-four, not are. Against by: dimensions take by (a three by five card, eight by ten glossies), multiplication takes times. Against the -fold suffix: threefold attaches to the number, three times is a phrase. ✗ The classic ambiguity: three times more than and three times as much as are used interchangeably in American English, but strictly the first means 4× and the second 3× — in careful writing use as much as, or give both numbers. Note that times in three times a week and at times is the ordinary plural noun, not this preposition.
entries.see also: by, minus, plus, over, to the power of, to

entries.meaning: Reads an exponent aloud. It is the one operator in this section that most Americans learned to say years before they learned to write it, which is why its clipped variants have largely taken the spoken form over.
examples: Two to the power of ten is one thousand twenty-four.
The population grows roughly as e to the power of the growth rate times time.
A byte holds two to the eighth distinct values.
Sound intensity falls off as distance to the power of minus two.
Ten to the power of six is a million, which is the conversion everybody memorizes and nobody quite trusts.
In the spreadsheet the formula reads A1^3, which you say aloud as A1 to the third power.
entries.pronunciation note: tuh thuh POW-er uhv; weak /tə ðə ˈpaʊɚ əv/, casually /tə ðə ˈpaʊɚ ə/ — only pow- carries stress, and everything on either side of it reduces
entries.русский: в степени: two to the power of ten — два в десятой степени
entries.register: neutral; the spoken form of an exponent, standard in teaching and in reading a formula aloud
entries.complement: a number or numeric expression, including a negative, a fraction, or a variable — four, minus two, one half, n. Never a gerund, never a finite clause. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: [base] to the power of [exponent] · [base] to the [ordinal] power · [base] to the [ordinal] (clipped) · [base] to the [variable]
entries.variants: American speech prefers the shorter shapes — ten to the fourth power, ten to the fourth, two to the n — and a scientist says ten to the ninth where a British textbook writes ten to the power of nine. At exponents two and three the phrase disappears in favor of squared and cubed. On the page it is a superscript, a caret (10^9), or e-notation (1e9).
entries.contrast: Against times and by a factor of: ten times three is thirty, ten to the power of three is a thousand — multiplication repeats addition, exponentiation repeats multiplication, and the gap between them opens fast. Against over, which reads the fraction bar rather than the exponent. The figurative use — bureaucracy to the power of ten — is a joke on the arithmetic, takes whatever number sounds worst, and does not survive into edited prose.
entries.see also: times, by a factor of, over, minus, per

entries.respell: uh MAT-er uhv; weak /ə ˈmædɚ əv/
entries.meaning: Puts a small number on something in order to say how little of it there was. The figure is real, but the smallness is the point, which is why the phrase resists any quantity a reader would consider substantial.
examples: The fire went through the attic in a matter of minutes.
The whole difference between the two bids is a matter of a few hundred dollars.
He missed the cut by a matter of inches.
In a matter of three weeks the neighborhood had collected the entire amount.
Getting the permit turned out to be a matter of two phone calls and a fax nobody could send.
Whether the levee holds is now a matter of hours, not days.
entries.pronunciation note: the t is a flap, so it sounds like madder — casually /ə ˈmædɚ ə/
entries.русский: всего-навсего, каких-нибудь — подчёркивает, что величина мала
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a small quantity, characteristically a stretch of time (a matter of minutes, a matter of a few dollars, a matter of inches). Never a gerund, never a finite clause in this sense. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: [clause] in a matter of [small quantity] · [be] a matter of [small quantity] · only a matter of [quantity]
entries.variants: in a matter of is the commonest full form and is the one that carries the time sense (in a matter of hours). It is only a matter of time is a frozen idiom meaning it will certainly happen eventually, and there the quantity is deliberately unstated.
entries.contrast: The measure sense always means only that much, never that much or more — it took a matter of minutes says the job was quick, and ✗ it took a matter of nine hours is odd because nine hours is not small. That is the whole rule, and it is why the phrase cannot carry a figure the reader would think large. Do not confuse it with the topic noun in a matter of principle, a matter of public record, a matter of opinion, which names a category rather than a quantity and belongs with the prepositions of reference at in the matter of. Against in the neighborhood of: that phrase hedges a figure it does not know, this one belittles a figure it does.
entries.see also: in the neighborhood of, shy of, within, the better part of, in the matter of

entries.meaning: Hedges a quantity by a small margin. It is the most frequent approximator in American English and the one that carries the least attitude: it makes no joke, claims no precision it does not have, and is at home anywhere from a text message to an annual report.
examples: About two hundred people showed up for a room booked for eighty.
The repair came to about nine hundred dollars.
The tank holds about twelve gallons, which gets you to Tucumcari and no farther.
Attendance was about half what it was in 2019.
He is about six two, give or take an inch of hair.
The two proposals cost about the same and differ in every other respect.
About one in five households in the county has no broadband at all.
entries.pronunciation note: the first syllable is a bare schwa, and the whole word clips to /baʊt/ in casual speech: 'bout a hundred people
entries.русский: около, примерно — нейтральное приближение, близко к названному числу
entries.register: neutral; the default hedge in both speech and writing
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a quantity — a number, a sum, a measure, an age, a proportion. Never a gerund and never a finite clause in this sense. It does not strand. Also an adverb of degree (about right, about finished, just about done), where it has no object at all, and that is the test. About to leave is a near-future construction, not a prepositional phrase; a book about running is the topic word, treated at about.
entries.pattern: about [number] · about [sum] · about [measure] · about as [adjective] as [noun phrase]
entries.variants: around is the interchangeable twin, a shade more casual. Approximately is the lab-report register, roughly the neutral written alternative, some the terse journalistic one (some 200 people). British round about two hundred is not American.
entries.contrast: This entry covers the quantity hedge; the clock-and-calendar hedge (about seven, about three weeks) is at about and the topic sense at about. About claims to be close to the number, which is what separates it from the rest of the family: in the neighborhood of claims only the right range, on the order of only the right power of ten. Two habits to avoid: do not hedge a figure that is already exact (about 217 people undercuts itself), and do not stack it on a range, which is already doing the hedging — write forty to fifty people, not about forty to fifty people.
entries.see also: around, in the neighborhood of, on the order of, upward of, about (time), about (topic)

entries.meaning: Hedges a quantity, informally. It is the spoken default — in conversation Americans reach for it about as often as for about, and the choice between the two is rhythm rather than meaning.
examples: The truck goes for around forty thousand new.
They are expecting around fifty people, which in that family means sixty-five.
The building is around a hundred years old and has the wiring to prove it.
Enrollment has held steady at around twelve hundred since the mill closed.
We ended up somewhere around eight hundred dollars over budget.
He weighed around two-forty when they signed him and around two-ninety when they cut him.
entries.pronunciation note: clipped to /raʊnd/ in casual speech: 'round fifty bucks
entries.русский: около, примерно — то же, что about, но разговорнее
entries.register: neutral to informal; a shade more casual than about
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a quantity, a sum, or a measure. Never a gerund, never a finite clause. It does not strand in this sense. Also an adverb and a verb particle (stick around, turn it around, the other way around), where it has no object — that is the test.
entries.pattern: around [number] · around [sum] · somewhere around [quantity]
entries.variants: round is the British form and is not American English. An American writer uses around for the preposition and reserves round for the noun, verb, and adjective (a round of drinks, round the numbers off, a round figure); the contraction 'round belongs to songs and speech, not to edited prose. Around is also the American choice in year-round, around the clock, and the other way around.
entries.contrast: Interchangeable with about for quantities, with a mild division of labor: about is commoner with measured amounts and in formal writing, around commoner in speech and with round figures. Both claim to be close to the number. Against in the neighborhood of: the long phrase widens the tolerance and adds a folksy tone. The spatial and movement senses (around the corner, around the lake) are at around; the clock-and-calendar sense is at around.
entries.see also: about, in the neighborhood of, upward of, around (movement), around (time)

entries.pronunciation note: at thee ik-SPENSS uhv; weak /ət ði ɪkˈspɛns əv/, casually /ət ði ɪkˈspɛns ə/
entries.русский: в ущерб чему-л.; за чей-л. счёт (об оплате); на чей-л. счёт (о насмешке)
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (at the expense of getting any sleep). Never a finite clause. In the payment sense a possessive replaces the of: at the taxpayers' expense, at his own expense.
entries.pattern: [clause] at the expense of [noun phrase / verb-ing] · [clause] at [possessive] expense
entries.variants: at the cost of — interchangeable in the sacrifice sense, and at a cost of is the only one of the family that takes a plain dollar figure (at a cost of $4 million).
entries.contrast: Three senses share a form. Sacrifice: speed at the expense of accuracy names what was given up. Payment: at the taxpayers' expense names who paid, and there the possessive is normal. Humiliation: a joke at his expense. Against to the tune of: both carry editorial weight, but to the tune of is about the size of a sum and this is about what the sum cost somebody.
entries.see also: in the amount of, to the tune of, for, in exchange for

entries.respell: in ik-SESS uhv; weak /ɪn ɪkˈsɛs əv/, casually /ɪn ɪkˈsɛs ə/
entries.meaning: Marks a quantity as exceeding a stated threshold, with the threshold treated as a boundary rather than an approximation. Everything above the line is included and nothing below it is.
examples: The settlement was reported to be in excess of four million dollars.
Speeds in excess of ninety miles an hour were recorded on that stretch of road.
Any amount in excess of the policy limit is the insured's own responsibility.
The building has stood for a period in excess of two centuries.
Loads in excess of four hundred pounds will void the warranty.
Applicants with in excess of ten years' service are exempt from the review.
entries.русский: свыше, более — офиц., юр.; твёрдая нижняя граница, а не оценка
entries.register: formal; legal, financial, and technical
entries.complement: noun phrase, essentially always a quantity or a named threshold. Never a gerund, never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [quantity] in excess of [threshold] · [clause] in excess of [quantity]
entries.contrast: A five-word way of saying more than, and in ordinary prose it should be cut: in excess of 200 people is more than 200 people. It earns its place in contracts and specifications, where over can be misread spatially and more than can sound like an estimate: amounts in excess of the deductible is unambiguous and amounts over the deductible is not quite. Against upward of: upward of is an estimate near the number, in excess of is a hard floor. Against north of: same meaning, opposite register.
entries.see also: over, north of, upward of, under, to the extent of

entries.meaning: Attaches an exact sum to a financial instrument or an obligation. It states the figure and takes no position on whether the figure is large.
examples: Enclosed is a check in the amount of twelve hundred dollars.
The court entered judgment in the amount of $84,317 plus costs.
We received an invoice in the amount of $2,415.60, which does not match the estimate.
A refund in the amount of the deposit will be issued within ten business days.
Bond was set in the amount of fifty thousand dollars.
The district issued notes in the total amount of nine million dollars.
entries.pronunciation note: in thee uh-MOWNT uhv; weak /ɪn ði əˈmaʊnt əv/, casually /ɪn ði əˈmaʊnt ə/
entries.русский: на сумму — канцеляр., юр.: чек, счёт, решение суда на такую-то сумму
entries.register: legal and commercial; distinctly American bureaucratic English
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a sum of money — figures or words. Never a gerund, never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [check / judgment / invoice / refund / bond] in the amount of [sum]
entries.variants: in the sum of — older, and commoner in British legal drafting. In the total amount of for aggregates. For alone is the plain-English replacement and the one federal plain-language guidance recommends.
entries.contrast: Pure legalese for for or of: a check in the amount of $500 is a check for $500 and nothing else. It survives because in a document that will be read adversarially it keeps the sum visibly separate from the instrument, and because forms have always been written this way. Against to the tune of: same territory, opposite register and opposite attitude — the legal phrase is scrupulously neutral, the journalistic one is not.
entries.see also: to the tune of, for, to the extent of, at the expense of

entries.meaning: Gives an approximate quantity while explicitly declining to be precise. The metaphor is spatial and does real work: a neighborhood is a region, not a point, and the phrase concedes that the speaker has not measured.
examples: Repairs will run in the neighborhood of three thousand dollars, maybe a little more.
They are expecting somewhere in the neighborhood of forty thousand people.
The engine puts out in the neighborhood of four hundred horsepower.
He has been doing this for something in the neighborhood of twenty years.
The house sold for something in the ballpark of what the appraiser had said.
Attendance was in the ballpark of what we saw last spring.
entries.pronunciation note: in thuh NAY-ber-hood uhv; weak /ɪn ðə ˈneɪbɚhʊd əv/, casually /ɪn ðə ˈneɪbɚhʊd ə/
entries.русский: где-то около, примерно — разг.-амер.; допуск шире, чем у about
entries.register: informal to neutral; distinctly American
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a quantity or a sum, or a fused relative standing in for one (in the neighborhood of what the appraiser said). Never a gerund, never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] in the neighborhood of [quantity] · somewhere in the neighborhood of [quantity]
entries.variants: in the ballpark of — more informal, also American, from the same family as a ballpark figure. In the region of and of the order of are the British equivalents and read as foreign in American copy. Somewhere in the neighborhood of is the usual full form in speech.
entries.contrast: A hedge with a wider tolerance than about and a friendlier tone than on the order of. The three make different claims about precision: about $200 claims to be close, in the neighborhood of $200 claims only the right range, on the order of $200 claims only the right power of ten. Because it is folksy, it is out of place in a document where the number matters.
entries.see also: about, around, on the order of, upward of, shy of

senses.head: Arithmetic subtraction; reduced by
examples: Nine minus four is five.
Net proceeds are the sale price minus commissions and closing costs.
Enter the gross figure minus the two adjustments on line nine.

senses.head: Below zero — temperatures and negative quantities
examples: It was minus twelve in Fargo the morning they left.
The freezer holds steady at minus eighteen Celsius.
The wind chill hit minus thirty and the district held classes anyway.

senses.head: Without; lacking
body: Informal, and usually a little comic.
examples: He came back from the trip minus a suitcase and one shoe.
They played the whole second half minus their two best defenders.
The band finished the tour minus a drummer and most of their gear.

entries.pronunciation note: no weak form; the second syllable is already a schwa and the first keeps its stress
entries.русский: минус — вычитание; ниже нуля (о температуре); разг. «без чего-л., лишившись чего-л.»
entries.register: neutral in arithmetic; informal in the lacking sense
entries.type: simple (Latin, the neuter of minor) — also a noun (a minus, the minuses outweigh the pluses) and an adjective (a minus sign, a B-minus), neither of which takes an object
entries.complement: noun phrase or numeral. Never a gerund, never a clause. It does not strand. In the temperature and negative-number use it is not really a preposition at all but part of the numeral, and there it takes no preceding quantity: minus forty, a minus sign.
entries.pattern: [number] minus [number] · [noun phrase] minus [noun phrase] · minus [number] (temperature)
entries.american temperature convention: minus ten in writing, ten below in speech, and negative ten in scientific and increasingly in general American use.
entries.contrast: Against plus: exact opposites in arithmetic and mirror images in the informal sense — the team minus its starting center against the team plus two draft picks. Against less: in commercial writing less is the standard subtractor for deductions (gross pay less withholding) and minus is the arithmetic one; the exception-marking senses of both are at less and minus.
entries.see also: plus, times, over, minus, less, without

entries.meaning: Reports a figure from which a named item has already been deducted. It is the word in a financial sentence that tells you whether you are looking at what was earned or at what is left, and misplacing it moves real money.
examples: The fund returned just over six percent last year, net of fees.
Proceeds net of closing costs came to a hundred and forty thousand.
The district's obligation is stated net of the state reimbursement.
Rent is nine hundred a month net of utilities, which the tenant pays directly.
Net of the one-time charge, operating income was actually up for the quarter.
Report the figure net of returns and allowances, not gross sales.
entries.pronunciation note: NET uhv; weak /ˈnɛt əv/, and at any speed the t flaps and the two words run together as /ˈnɛdə/ — NED-uh — net of taxes comes out NED-uh taxes, which is why the phrase is so easy to miss in a spoken briefing
entries.русский: за вычетом — о цифре, из которой названное уже вычтено (не «включая»)
entries.register: formal; accounting, finance, tax, and contract drafting — an American meets it on a closing statement, in a fund prospectus, on a pay stub, and in a commercial lease
entries.type: complex (adjective + fixed of) — bare net is also an adjective (net income, net weight), a noun, an adverb (it comes to four hundred net), and a verb (the sale netted him twelve thousand), none of which takes a prepositional object
entries.complement: noun phrase naming what has been subtracted — a tax, a fee, a cost, a discount, a reserve, an allowance. Never a gerund: ✗ net of paying the commissions → net of commissions. Never a finite clause. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: [figure] net of [deduction] · [verb of reporting] [figure] net of [deduction] · [proceeds / return / income] net of [deduction]
entries.variants: after is the plain-English equivalent and what a prospectus writes for a lay reader (returns after fees); less is the older commercial subtractor (gross pay less withholding); gross of is the opposite number and lives almost entirely in investment reporting.
entries.contrast: It reports a subtraction that has already happened, which is the whole difference between it and minus or less — those perform one in front of you. The expensive misreading is taking it for including: a fund returning seven percent net of fees has already paid itself, so seven is what the investor keeps, while seven percent gross of fees is the number before the cut, and the gap between the two is the fee. Against exclusive of: that says an item was never in the figure at all; net of says it was in and has been taken out. Against after: after is chronological in ordinary English and only borrows this arithmetic sense inside a small set of financial phrases.
entries.see also: minus, less, exclusive of, in excess of, at the expense of

entries.respell: NORTH uhv; weak /ˈnɔrθ əv/, casually /ˈnɔrθ ə/
entries.meaning: Puts a quantity above a stated number, informally and with a note of relish. The number named is almost always a round one, and the point is usually that it is impressively or scandalously large.
examples: The contract is reportedly worth north of forty million dollars.
He was still throwing north of ninety-five in the eighth inning.
Redoing the kitchen alone will run north of thirty thousand.
She is north of sixty and still runs half marathons.
Turnout came in south of what the campaign had been promising all month.
The stock closed south of nine dollars for the first time since 2019.
entries.русский: больше чем, за отметку — разг.-журн., с оттенком «внушительно много»; south of — меньше
entries.register: informal; journalistic, especially in business and sports writing; American
entries.type: complex — bare north is a noun, an adjective, and an adverb (due north, the north side, drive north), none of which takes an object; only north of is the preposition
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a quantity — a sum, a number, an age, a speed — or a fused relative standing in for one (south of what the campaign was promising). Never a gerund, never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] north of [quantity] · [noun phrase] north of [quantity]
entries.variants: south of — the mirror image, meaning less than, slightly less common and with the same swagger.
entries.contrast: A live metaphor from the map, where north is up the page: north of $2 million is more than $2 million. Keep it out of formal writing, where in excess of or plain more than belongs, and keep it well away from actual geography, where north of Denver means exactly what it says and a reader will take it literally. Against upward of: upward of is an estimate, north of asserts a floor with attitude.
entries.see also: in excess of, over, under, upward of, shy of

examples: The device draws on the order of two watts in standby.

entries.pronunciation note: on thee OR-der uhv; weak /ən ði ˈɔrdɚ əv/, casually /ən ði ˈɔrdɚ ə/
entries.русский: порядка (величины) — научн.; также «вроде, наподобие» чего-л.
entries.register: formal; scientific and technical
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a quantity, usually a round number or a power of ten; in the second sense, a noun phrase naming a kind of thing. Never a gerund, never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] on the order of [quantity] · [noun phrase] on the order of [noun phrase]
entries.variants: of the order of is the standard British form and in the order of is also British and criticized there. American English uses on the order of. None of them is in order to, and none is in the order of meaning in the sequence of.
entries.contrast: In physics and engineering it has a technical meaning — within a factor of ten of — so on the order of a thousand legitimately covers a few hundred to a few thousand. In general prose it has weakened to approximately, and a scientific reader will still hear the stronger claim. Against in the neighborhood of: the neighborhood form is folksy and implies a narrower range. The second sense, something on the order of a memoir, is a manner use rather than a measure one and means of the kind of.
entries.see also: in the neighborhood of, upward of, in excess of, about, around

examples: Over two hundred people showed up for a meeting the room was booked for forty.

senses.head: Exceeding a budget, a limit, or a standard
examples: The project came in three weeks late and over budget.
We are eight hundred dollars over for the month and it is the fourteenth.
He was doing eighty in a fifty-five — twenty-five over.

examples: Three over four is the same as seventy-five percent.

senses.head: Through a channel of transmission — the medium sense
body: The complement is the wire, the air, or the service that carried it.
examples: He gave notice over the phone, which his father never forgave.

Nothing sensitive goes over email, and nothing at all goes over the hotel's wifi.

entries.pronunciation note: no weak form; the second syllable is a syllabic /ɚ/, and the flapped over a runs together as /ˈoʊvɚɹə/
entries.русский: свыше, больше; сверх (бюджета, лимита); дробное «делить на»; по (телефону, почте)
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or a numeral; in the medium sense, a channel noun that normally keeps its article (over the phone, over the air, over a secure line). Never a gerund in any of the senses below and never a finite clause — the gerund-taking sense (sued over failing to disclose the defect) is the cause preposition at over. It strands (the number we came in over, what did you hear it over?), and it is also an adverb and a particle (Come over, It's over, turn it over), where it has no object — that is the test.
entries.pattern: [verb] over [quantity] · [be] over [budget / limit] · [number] over [number] (a fraction) · [verb of communication] over [the channel]
entries.contrast: This entry covers the excess-of-quantity senses and the transmission-medium sense. The others are spread across the catalog: the spatial senses at over, the span-of-time and simultaneity senses at over, the trigger-of-conflict sense at over, the preference sense (chose Denver over Phoenix) at over, and the topic sense (a fight over money) at over. Against more than: the old rule that over cannot mean more than with numbers was dropped by the AP Stylebook in 2014 and was never grounded in real usage — both are correct and always were. Against above: with plain counts over is the default (over sixty people), while above is preferred when the number sits on a named scale (above 30,000 feet, above average, above freezing). Against under: exact opposites here. The medium sense against the time sense: over dinner names a stretch of time you can measure, but over the phone names a channel and no stretch of anything — which is why we settled it over the phone in four minutes is fine and ✗ we settled it over dinner in four minutes is not. Against on: on the phone is the state of being connected, over the phone is the route the words took, so she's on the phone but he told me over the phone.
entries.see also: under, in excess of, north of, upward of, via, through, over (movement), over (time), over (cause), over (topic)

examples: Four plus four is eight.
Enter the base salary plus any bonus in the second column.
Rent is eleven hundred a month plus utilities.
The fare is thirty dollars plus tip.
The venue holds five hundred plus.
She has thirty-plus years of classroom experience.

senses.head: Arithmetic addition; increased by
examples: Four plus four is eight.
Enter the base salary plus any bonus in the second column.

senses.head: With the addition of — the price-and-package sense
examples: Rent is eleven hundred a month plus utilities.
The fare is thirty dollars plus tip.

senses.head: Postpositive: and more; at least that much
examples: The venue holds five hundred plus.
She has thirty-plus years of classroom experience.

entries.pronunciation note: no weak form; it is stressed even in four plus four, which is what keeps it audible in dictation
entries.русский: плюс — сложение; плюс к тому (цена плюс налог); постпозитивно «с лишним»
entries.register: neutral in arithmetic and pricing; informal as a sentence connector
entries.type: simple (Latin, "more") — also a noun (a real plus, the pluses outweigh the minuses), an adjective (a plus sign, a B-plus), and a coordinating conjunction (Plus, it's cheaper), none of which takes a prepositional object
entries.complement: noun phrase or numeral. Never a gerund in the arithmetic sense. The informal Plus, it's cheaper takes a whole clause, but that is a coordinating conjunction, not this preposition. It does not strand. Postpositively it attaches to a number with no complement at all: fifty-plus, a B-plus, thirty years plus.
entries.pattern: [number] plus [number] · [noun phrase] plus [noun phrase] · [number]-plus (postpositive) · Plus, [clause] (informal conjunction)
entries.contrast: Against minus: the arithmetic opposites. Against and: a plus phrase does not make a singular subject plural — The base rate plus the surcharge is eighty dollars, singular, is the careful form, exactly as with along with and as well as. The additive and accompaniment senses are at plus. Against positive: for temperatures, American English says ten above or simply ten, never ✗ plus ten, which is a European convention.
entries.see also: minus, times, plus, with, along with

entries.respell: SHY uhv; weak /ˈʃaɪ əv/, casually /ˈʃaɪ ə/
entries.meaning: Places a quantity just below a target, with the implication that the target was the thing being aimed at. The gap is small by definition, and naming it is most of the point.
examples: He died two weeks shy of his ninetieth birthday.
The bill came in just shy of four hundred dollars.
She finished a tenth of a second shy of the school record.
We ended up three votes shy of a majority.
The tank was a gallon shy of full when we got back.
The bid came in just shy of what the board had authorized.
entries.русский: не доходя до, чуть меньше: just shy of — «чуть-чуть не дотянув до»
entries.register: informal to neutral; American
entries.type: complex (adjective + fixed of) — bare shy is an ordinary adjective (a shy child, don't be shy) and takes no object
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a quantity, an age, or a point in time, or a fused relative standing in for one (just shy of what the board had authorized). Never a gerund, never a finite clause. It is nearly always preceded by a measure of the shortfall or by just.
entries.pattern: [size of shortfall] shy of [target] · just shy of [quantity]
entries.contrast: Means short of, not quite up to. Unlike short of, it has none of the exception senses: ✗ shy of a miracle, we are finished. Just shy of is by far the commonest form and hedges downward — just shy of a million is a little under a million. Note the collocational quirk: the phrase wants a measured gap in front of it, so shy of forty alone is odd where two months shy of forty is idiomatic. Against under and less than, which state a range; shy of states a near miss.
entries.see also: short of, under, within, to within, north of, a matter of

entries.respell: thuh BET-er PART uhv; weak /ðə ˈbɛdɚ pɑrt əv/
entries.meaning: Names most of a quantity while conceding it was not all of it. Whoever writes the better part of a million is telling you the figure did not quite get there.
examples: They spent the better part of a year waiting on the environmental review.
He drove the better part of four hundred miles without stopping once.
The better part of the crop was in the ground before the rain came.
The hearing took up the better part of two days and settled nothing.
She has lived on that street for the best part of thirty years.
Redoing the second floor ate the better part of the bequest.
entries.pronunciation note: the t of better flaps — casually /ðə ˈbɛdɚ pɑrt ə/
entries.русский: бо́льшая часть, почти весь — здесь better значит «бо́льший», а не «лучший»
entries.register: neutral; faintly literary
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a divisible quantity — a stretch of time, a sum, a distance, a countable population. Never a gerund, never a finite clause. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: [verb of spending or lasting] the better part of [quantity] · for the better part of [stretch of time]
entries.variants: the best part of is the British form and turns up in American speech as well; the greater part of is the formal one; most of is the plain replacement and is shorter every single time.
entries.contrast: It means most of, not the superior half of. The better is a fossil comparative meaning larger, the same one buried in the better half of the field, so the better part of an hour is about fifty minutes and says nothing about their quality. Two rules keep it honest: the complement has to be divisible (✗ the better part of a decision), and the phrase claims more than half and less than all, so it cannot be stacked on a hedge — ✗ about the better part of a year. Against about: about a year may be over or under, the better part of a year is always under, which makes it a downward hedge from a round number. Do not confuse it with the proverb discretion is the better part of valor, where part means component and the whole thing is a different idiom.
entries.see also: about, in the neighborhood of, shy of, a matter of, under

examples: Each partner is liable to the extent of his capital contribution and no further.
The policy covers water damage to the extent of fifty thousand dollars.
The town rebuilt the levee to the extent of its available funds.
He backed her to the extent of putting his own name on the loan.
She disagreed, to the extent of filing a written dissent.

senses.head: Up to a stated limit; to the maximum of
examples: Each partner is liable to the extent of his capital contribution and no further.

entries.pronunciation note: tuh thee ik-STENT uhv; weak /tə ði ɪkˈstɛnt əv/, casually /tə ði ɪkˈstɛnt ə/ — both the to and the of reduce, and only -tent- carries stress
entries.русский: в пределах, в размере (верхний предел); вплоть до того, что
entries.register: formal; legal and insurance drafting
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (to the extent of resigning). Never a finite clause — with a clause the phrase changes shape to to the extent that, which is a subordinating conjunction and a different item.
entries.pattern: [clause] to the extent of [quantity / noun phrase / verb-ing] · compare the conjunction: to the extent that [clause]
entries.contrast: Two readings sorted by the complement. With a number it is a measure and a ceiling: liable to the extent of $50,000 means that is the maximum. With an abstract noun or a gerund it means as far as, going so far as to: he backed her to the extent of resigning. Do not blur it into to the extent that, which introduces a clause and functions as a conditional (to the extent that funds are available = insofar as). Against in the amount of: that phrase fixes an exact sum, this one fixes an upper bound.
entries.see also: in the amount of, in excess of, up to, within

entries.meaning: Attaches a large sum to an action while signaling disapproval or astonishment. The metaphor is that the payer is dancing to somebody else's music.
examples: Taxpayers subsidized the stadium to the tune of three hundred million dollars.
The firm was fined to the tune of eleven million for the disclosure failures.
He ran up credit card debt to the tune of sixty thousand dollars in under two years.
The district overspent its transportation budget to the tune of about four million.
The settlement compensated the plaintiffs to the tune of twelve thousand dollars apiece.
The state has backstopped the fund to the tune of a billion and a half since 2018.
entries.pronunciation note: tuh thuh TOON uhv; weak /tə ðə ˈtun əv/, casually /tə ðə ˈtun ə/
entries.русский: на кругленькую сумму в… — журн.; всегда с оттенком осуждения или изумления
entries.register: informal to neutral; journalistic
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a sum of money, characteristically a large one. Never a gerund, never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] to the tune of [sum]
entries.contrast: Not a neutral way of stating an amount. It always carries an editorial nudge — that the sum is outrageous, wasteful, or improbably large. If you want the figure to land neutrally, use of or for; if you are drafting a document, use in the amount of. It resists small numbers, which is a reliable test: ✗ fined to the tune of forty dollars is comic rather than damning. The literal musical sense (sing it to the tune of "Yankee Doodle") is ordinary to plus a noun, not this idiom.
entries.see also: in the amount of, at the expense of, in excess of, for

entries.meaning: Marks how close a process or measurement came to a target. The to supplies the movement and the within supplies the margin, which is why neither works alone in these sentences.
examples: The part is machined to within half a thousandth of an inch.
The final polls had it to within two points of the actual result.
They climbed to within a hundred yards of the summit before turning back.
Our estimate turned out to be good to within about five percent.
The clock keeps time to within a second a month.
The probe mapped the ridge to within a few centimeters of vertical accuracy.
entries.русский: с точностью до — насколько близко измерение или движение подошло к цели
entries.register: neutral to formal; technical
entries.type: complex (a preposition stacked on a preposition)
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a tolerance — a distance, a margin, a percentage. Never a gerund, never a finite clause. A trailing of + target is usually obligatory.
entries.pattern: [verb of measuring or approaching] to within [tolerance] of [target]
entries.contrast: One of the small set of stacked prepositions English allows (from behind the door, except in an emergency, until after lunch). It differs from plain within by adding a movement or a measurement that closes on the target: accurate within a millimeter states a standing property, machined to within a millimeter states a result that was achieved. Against shy of: shy of names a shortfall from a goal, to within names a tolerance around a target.
entries.see also: within, shy of, to, within

entries.pronunciation note: no weak form; before a vowel the r links and the d flaps, so under an hour comes out /ˈʌndɚɹən ˈaʊɚ/
entries.русский: меньше, менее; в пределах (бюджета, нормы); младше (столько-то лет)
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or a numeral. Never a gerund in this sense, never a finite clause. It strands marginally (the figure we came in under) and is also an adverb (The whole block went under), where it has no object.
entries.pattern: [verb] under [quantity] · [be / come in] under [budget / limit] · under [age]
entries.contrast: This entry covers the below-a-quantity senses; the spatial sense is at under. Against less than: interchangeable with plain numbers (under fifty people, less than fifty people), though fewer than is the fussier choice for things you can count. Against below: under for plain quantities and thresholds, below for named scales and reference lines (below freezing, below sea level, below average, below cost). Against over: exact opposites. Note the separate subject to sense — under warranty, under oath, under contract, under anesthesia — which is not a measure at all.
entries.see also: over, within, shy of, in excess of, under

entries.respell: UHP-werd uhv; weak /ˈʌpwɚd əv/, casually /ˈʌpwɚd ə/
entries.meaning: Places a quantity at or approaching a stated number. It is the most ambiguous of the measure prepositions, and the only one in this section whose two readings point in opposite directions — which is why it should be replaced whenever the exact reading matters and left alone when it does not.
examples: The repair will take upward of six hours, so plan on the whole day.
Upward of twelve thousand people applied for four hundred jobs.
The equipment costs upward of a quarter of a million dollars.
They lost upward of half their inventory in the flood.
She has upwards of thirty years in the same building.
The hearing ran upward of five hours with no break.
entries.pronunciation note: which is why the -s of upwards is so easy to lose in speech and so audible on the page
entries.русский: свыше; или почти, до — двусмысленно: два прочтения указывают в разные стороны
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a quantity. Never a gerund, never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] upward of [quantity] · [noun phrase] upward of [quantity]
entries.variants: upwards of — the dominant British form and common in American writing too. American style guides prefer upward of, in line with the general American preference for toward, forward, backward, and afterward without the -s.
entries.contrast: Two competing readings, and this is the word's real problem. Historically and in careful usage it means more than (upward of a thousand = over a thousand); in a great deal of current American writing it means approaching, as much as (upward of a thousand = nearly a thousand). A reader cannot tell which you intend, so when the difference matters write more than or nearly. Against in excess of, which is unambiguously a floor, and north of, which is the informal version of the same claim.
entries.see also: in excess of, north of, over, in the neighborhood of, on the order of

entries.pronunciation note: with-IN; also /wɪˈθɪn/ for some American speakers. No weak form — the stress is on the second syllable, and the with- inside it does not reduce to /wəθ/ the way free-standing with does
entries.русский: в пределах, не выходя за (допуск, бюджет, право); в радиусе (расстояния)
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun. Never a gerund and never a finite clause — ✗ within finishing the job, ✗ within we agreed. It does not strand. It is also an adverb in legal and literary English (see within, the terms set out within), where it has no object.
entries.pattern: [be / fall] within [tolerance or limit] · [verb] within [margin] of [target] · within [budget / reason / reach / one's rights]
entries.contrast: This entry covers the tolerance, limit, and distance senses; the deadline sense (within two weeks) is at within. Against to within: within states a standing range, to within states a result measured up to a margin. Against in: in tolerance is shop floor talk and within tolerance is the written form; inside is spatial only. Against under, a real distinction: under budget means you spent less than the budget, within budget means you did not exceed it — and within includes spending every last dollar.
entries.see also: to within, under, in, within, inside of
